t: Monotone Increasing Digits — Greedy Digit Repair
o: We must find the largest number ≤ n whose digits never decrease left to right. If n itself is monotone increasing (like 1234), the answer is n. Otherwise, some digit is larger than the digit after it; the best fix is to decrement that digit and turn everything after it into 9s, since trailing 9s are the largest possible suffix and keep the number as big as possible while staying valid. With n up to 10^9 (at most 10 digits), even a brute force over candidates would be too slow if done naively by scanning all numbers, so we work directly on the digits in O(d) time.
k: Scan digits left to right; find the first position where digits[i] > digits[i+1] — that's the violation to repair.
When repairing at index i, we may need to also decrement earlier equal digits (e.g. 332 → 299), so walk i back while digits[i-1] == digits[i].
After decrementing digits[i], set every digit after it to '9' for the largest valid result.

a.i: Check numbers from n downward and return the first one with monotone increasing digits. It's simple but can be slow: e.g. n = 10^9 has answer 999999999, requiring ~1 step, but cases like n = 123456788 require only small scans, while worst cases like n = 1000000000 scan down to 999999999 — about 10^8 iterations, which may TLE depending on limits. Included mainly to motivate the greedy.
s: Define a helper that checks whether an integer's digits are non-decreasing.
Iterate candidate from n down to 0.
Return the first candidate passing the check.
a.t: O(n · d) worst case where d ≈ 10 digits per check — far too slow when the gap between n and its answer is large.
a.sp: O(d) for the digit string of each candidate.

a.i: Convert n to a digit array and find the first index i where digits[i] > digits[i+1]. To maximize the result, decrement digits[i]; but if the previous digit equals digits[i] (e.g. "332"), decrementing only position i gives "322" which still violates monotonicity, so move i left past all equal digits. Then fill everything right of i with 9s. This yields the largest valid number because the prefix before i is untouched, position i drops by exactly 1, and 9s are the maximal possible tail.
s: Convert n to a character/digit array s of length d.
Scan from left; find the first i with s[i] > s[i+1]. If none exists, return n unchanged.
While i > 0 and s[i-1] == s[i], decrement i (handle runs of equal digits).
Set all positions j > i to '9' and parse back to an integer.
a.t: O(d) where d ≤ 10 is the number of digits — two linear passes plus a fill.

w: Always present the greedy approach in an interview; mention brute force only briefly to show why it fails on large gaps. Key pitfalls: forgetting to walk back through runs of equal digits (332 must become 299, not 322... wait, 322 isn't valid — you'd get 329→ wrong; correct handling gives 299), and remembering that if n is already monotone increasing you must return n exactly. Edge cases: n = 0 (answer 0), single-digit n (always itself), and n like 1000000000 whose answer 999999999 fits in a 32-bit int. Likely follow-ups: prove correctness of the greedy (exchange argument: any valid number ≤ n either shares the prefix before the first violation or must drop an earlier digit, making it smaller than our construction), or handle inputs given as strings beyond 64-bit range — the same algorithm works verbatim.
